title: The Fosbury Flop
text:
In the 1960s the standard way to clear a high jump bar was the straddle, in which the athlete went over face down, rolling his body around the bar. Before that, many had used the scissors kick. Dick Fosbury, a high school jumper in Medford, Oregon, could not master the straddle. Using the older scissors style, he began leaning back further and further as he went over, until he was clearing the bar head first and on his back, arching over it and landing on his shoulders.

Coaches were doubtful, and some found the technique ridiculous. A local newspaper described him as flopping over the bar, and the name stuck. But the method worked for Fosbury, and it became possible at all only because schools were replacing sawdust and sand landing pits with deep foam mats, which made landing on the back safe.

Fosbury kept improving at Oregon State University and won the national college title. At the 1968 Olympic Games in Mexico City he won the gold medal with a jump of 2.24 meters, an Olympic record, in front of a worldwide television audience that had never seen anything like it. Within about a decade, most of the world's top high jumpers had adopted the flop, and today it is almost universal.
lesson: The accepted method is not always the best one; it may only be the one everyone learned. When conditions change, a different approach can overtake the old standard.
source: Official results of the 1968 Olympic Games; contemporary press reports
